short: A last Roman-barbarian coalition stopped Attila's invasion of Gaul in one of antiquity's largest battles.
full:
Attila the Hun invaded Gaul in 451 with an army drawn from Huns and subject Germanic peoples, sacking cities along the way. The Western Roman general Flavius Aetius, unable to face him alone, assembled a coalition of Visigoths under King Theodoric I, along with Franks, Burgundians and other federate forces, and intercepted Attila near Chalons, in the Catalaunian Plains of modern north-eastern France.

The battle on 20 June 451 was enormous and bloody, and casualty figures in ancient sources run to tens of thousands; Theodoric I was killed, reportedly trampled after falling from his horse. Attila withdrew from Gaul, and though he invaded Italy the following year, he never again threatened the West at this scale before his death in 453. It was the last major campaign in which Western Roman forces and Germanic allies fought together as a coalition rather than as rivals.
